source.title: SmoothLLM: Defending Large Language Models Against Jailbreaking Attacks
source.authors: Alexander Robey; Eric Wong; Hamed Hassani; George Pappas

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates adversarial jailbreak prompts against safety-aligned chat models and reports harmful-response rates. This tests the suffix-bypass behavior using attack success rates, while its main intervention is an inference-time randomized defense, not fine-tuning or a token-distribution measurement.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the study's GCG adversarial-suffix results and the directly reported PAIR results, which use a different attack type. It does not test fine-tuning, per-token KL, compliant-opening prefills, decoding changes, localization in weights, or training methods for deepening safety. Figure 1 and Figure 14 also report attack results; the rows below use the explicit numerical table and text results with clearer condition-to-value mapping.
record.test_reason: A defense paper, but it reports undefended GCG adversarial-suffix attack success rates (ASR) on safety-trained chat models (Llama2-7b-chat, GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Claude, PaLM-2) and on Vicuna-13b. These bear on V4's suffix clause. The test is borderline: the undefended numbers are reproductions of GCG serving as the defense's baseline, and the paper does not address the shallow-alignment mechanism. Classed T3 rather than T2, since the study is not aimed at the claim's question. The SmoothLLM and perturbation results measure the defense or suffix fragility, not whether suffixes defeat refusal.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that adversarial suffixes are brittle to character-level perturbation and that SmoothLLM reduces GCG, PAIR, Random Search and AmpleGCG ASR with a small, non-negligible nominal-performance trade-off. They also claim resistance to adaptive GCG. They draw no conclusion about the depth of safety alignment.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates inference-time random character perturbation and output aggregation as a jailbreak defense. It does not reproduce the fine-tuning or token-position measurements in the claim's original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success changes with perturbation type, perturbation percentage q, sample count N, target model, attack method, and dataset. The paper also uses different jailbreak judges for GCG, PAIR, Random Search, and AmpleGCG.

fits_no_version.finding: GCG adversarial suffixes lose most of their attack success when about 10% of their characters are randomly perturbed.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimized adversarial suffixes are brittle: small character-level changes restore refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: An inference-time randomized smoothing defense lowers GCG and PAIR ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Input perturbation with majority voting mitigates jailbreaks at some cost to nominal performance.

fits_no_version.finding: PAIR semantic jailbreaks have model-dependent ASR.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Semantic jailbreaks elicit harmful output from some aligned models.

record.problems: The paper notes a non-negligible nominal-performance trade-off, and that large perturbations can make prompts incoherent and create false-positive jailbreak classifications. Some reported attack experiments are single-trial (Appendix B.11); uncertainty is not reported for the Table 7 ASRs.
record.rows_left_out: Other ASR results are shown in Figures 1, 7, 8, 10, and 14, and Tables 6 and 8. They were not separately extracted where they add further model-transfer, hyperparameter-sweep, adaptive-attack, or defense-variant conditions beyond the clearer tabulated and explicitly described results above. The paper's non-GCG attack results are represented here only for PAIR in Table 7.

untested.parts: Prefilling a compliant opening and decoding changes. Only adversarial suffixes (GCG, plus Random Search and AmpleGCG in Figure 1) are tested.

missing.what: Undefended ASR of suffixes transferred to closed models. Vicuna-source suffixes: GPT-3.5 28.7, GPT-4 5.6, Claude-1 1.3, Claude-2 1.6, PaLM-2 24.9. Llama2-source suffixes: 16.6, 2.7, 0.5, 0.9, 27.9.
Undefended ASR of Random Search and AmpleGCG (both suffix-type attacks) on Vicuna, Llama2, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. The figure values are hard to map to bars.

record.verdict_notes: Vicuna-13b-v1.5 has limited safety training, so its high ASR is weak evidence about safety-trained models. GCG ASR uses a refusal-keyword judge, which the authors note produces false positives; the undefended ASR also depends on this judge. GPT-4's low GCG ASR is attributed by the authors to likely vendor patches. The record's T2 is changed to T3 because the paper is a defense study whose undefended numbers are incidental reproductions.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning, example counts, and removal of refusal after training.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL or other measurements of aligned-versus-base output distributions across response positions.
Prefilled compliant openings and decoding changes; the study tests adversarial suffix attacks, not those mechanisms.
Whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety shallowness.
Training to deepen safety and whether deeper safety holds up.

reader_labels.condition: Unprotected GCG suffix attacks on Vicuna and GPT-3.5 in JBB-Behaviors, and unperturbed GCG suffixes on Vicuna and Llama2 in AdvBench
reader_labels.reason: The reported ASRs show that the tested suffix attacks produce harmful responses, with especially high rates on Vicuna and GPT-3.5 (r1, r5, r17, r18).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: GCG suffixes on Llama2 and GPT-4 in JBB-Behaviors; character-perturbed suffixes; and GCG with SmoothLLM
reader_labels.reason: Attack rates are low on some undefended models, character perturbations at q=10% reduce ASR below 1%, and SmoothLLM substantially reduces rates in several settings (r2-r4, r6-r8, r10-r16, r19-r26).
